That pattern leads to tight coupling and weak encapsulation — the behavior lives in the wrong place. You will learn how to detect this smell in real code, how to decide the method's rightful home, and how the Move Method and Move Field refactorings restore cohesion by placing behavior next to the data it needs. Module 07 › Chapter 7.5 › Feature Envy
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Feature Envy

When a method is more interested in another class's data than its own.

Chapter 7.5 • 16:9
Why this matters

Methods that live in the wrong class create brittle dependencies. Moving behavior back to the owning data keeps responsibilities clear and reduces breaks when internals change.

What you'll practice
  • Detect Feature Envy by looking for repeated accessor calls to another object.
  • Move methods into the class that owns the data.
  • Move fields when another class primarily uses that data.
Coming up

Python code walkthroughs, refactor step checklists, and testing strategies to keep behavior stable.

Visual Concept
Behavior should sit next to the data it operates on. If a method accesses another object's internals often, the method likely belongs there.
Explore Key Topics
Practice examples: Product pricing, Order totals, API compatibility when moving methods.
Duration: ~10–12 minutes of practice and code editing.

Third and fourth, you'll apply two refactorings: Move Method and Move Field. screens.title: How you'll practice
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond knowing the theory, you will follow a safe, repeatable sequence for moving methods and fields. Start by writing or verifying tests that cover the method's behavior. Next, duplicate the method into the target class and adapt references to use local fields rather than getters. Run tests: if green, remove the original method or replace it with a simple forwarder to preserve A P I compatibility. For moving a field, update constructors and access points, and be mindful of creating circular references. We'll practice with two concrete Python examples: a Product and DiscountCalculator pair, and an Order plus OrderProcessor. These examples let you see both simple and slightly more complex cases where multiple supporting methods and fields need migration. We'll also cover when Extract Class is a better choice if a method uses data from several classes equally. Practicing this sequence repeatedly makes refactoring low-risk and routine, so the codebase becomes easier to evolve over time.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.5 › Practice Sequence

Refactor Checklist

A short, repeatable process to apply Move Method or Move Field safely.

1. Tests

Ensure the method is covered so behavioral changes are caught quickly.

2. Duplicate

Copy the method into the target class and adapt to use local state.

3. Test

Run tests. If failures occur, adjust logic and dependencies carefully.

4. Clean

Remove old code or add a thin forwarding method for compatibility.

When to Extract Class

If behavior depends equally on several classes, create a new collaborator instead of moving into one home.

Avoiding Circularity

Move fields carefully and check dependencies to prevent classes from requiring each other.

Misconception

Moving code always reduces complexity. Not always — sometimes a new helper or Extract Class is the better design.

screens.title: What is Feature Envy?
screens.narratorSegment: Feature Envy is a code smell where a method in one class is more interested in another class's internals than its own. Practically, you see a method that calls many accessors on a foreign object, rarely using its own fields. This signals the method likely belongs to the other class. For example, a method that repeatedly calls product. get_price(), product. get_discount(), and product. get_name() while holding no relevant state itself demonstrates envy. The behavior indicates a misplaced responsibility. A simple detection strategy is to count how often the method touches another object's data versus its own; if the foreign touches dominate, you have Feature Envy. A common misconception is that adding a helper or utility class is always the solution. Often the correct answer is to move the method to the class whose data it uses — that preserves encapsulation and reduces accessors. Another contrast: if a method uses multiple classes equally, moving it into one will create new coupling; in that case consider Extract Class instead. In short, Feature Envy shows that behavior and data are separated incorrectly — your refactor moves behavior back next to its natural data owner. Think of it as returning work to the owner who has the tools and access to do it correctly.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Feature Envy: a method that primarily interacts with another object's data, suggesting it belongs elsewhere.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.5 › What is Feature Envy?
Definition & Detection

A method shows Feature Envy when it calls many accessors on another object and uses little of its own state. Count foreign accesses versus local uses to detect it.

Detection heuristic
  • Look for repeated calls like obj.get_...()
  • Check for empty host class state
  • Ask: would this method be simpler in the other class?
Concrete example
A Billing class method that frequently calls customer.get_address(), customer.get_tax_id(), and customer.get_discount() is a sign the calculation belongs with Customer or a dedicated BillingInfo object.
Common misconception
Moving code is always best. Sometimes an Extract Class preserves clarity when multiple collaborators are involved.
Spotting in code
def calculate_final_price(self, product):
    base = product.get_price()
    discount = base * product.get_discount()
    return base - discount
This method lives on a calculator but mostly reads product. It likely belongs on Product instead.
Key Takeaway

If behavior touches another object's internals frequently, move the behavior to that object's class when appropriate.

screens.title: Why Feature Envy hurts
screens.narratorSegment: Feature Envy undermines two core design goals: low coupling and strong encapsulation. When methods live in the wrong class, other classes must know about internal fields and accessors, which ties their implementation details together. If Class A repeatedly inspects Class B's internals, a change to B's data representation may require coordinated edits in A, increasing maintenance cost and the risk of bugs. Encapsulation is weakened because the external class is effectively manipulating the internal state rather than asking the owning class to perform the operation. This reduces clarity about who controls the data and where business rules belong. A helpful contrast is to consider the refactored alternative: move the behavior inside the data owner. Then changes to data layout are localized and the public interface presents a meaningful operation rather than raw access. A common misconception is that writing lots of getters is harmless; in reality getters encourage external classes to implement logic on foreign data instead of delegating the work to the object that owns it. The takeaway is clear: reduce Feature Envy to keep the system modular and resilient to internal change.

keyIdea.title: Negative Effects
keyIdea.text: Feature Envy increases coupling and weakens encapsulation, making maintenance and evolution harder.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.5 › Why it hurts
Comparison: Before vs After
Before: High coupling

Methods in Class A call many accessors on Class B. Changes in B force edits in A.

After: Encapsulated behavior

Behavior moved into Class B. B owns the logic and internal representation changes are localized.

Practical cost

More code to change, higher risk of bugs, and harder reasoning about where a responsibility lives.

Support: Example & Misconception

Example: A ReportGenerator that repeatedly calls employee.get_salary(), employee.get_bonus(), and employee.get_tax_code() should likely be refactored so Employee exposes a business operation like calculate_pay.

Misconception: "We just need utility classes." Utilities can hide misplaced responsibility. Prefer moving behavior to the object that owns its data when appropriate.

Key Takeaway

Feature Envy increases the surface area for bugs and makes evolving types more expensive. Move behavior to the data owner to reduce that surface area.

screens.title: Move Method — step-by-step
screens.narratorSegment: Move Method is a focused refactoring: relocate a method from one class to the class whose data it uses. Follow a safe sequence. Step one: ensure you have tests that cover the method's behavior. Tests act as a safety net. Step two: copy the method into the target class and modify it to use local fields and methods instead of foreign accessors. Step three: run tests. If tests pass, adjust call sites to invoke the new location. Step four: remove the original method or leave a thin forwarding method for backward compatibility while deprecating the old signature. Watch for related methods and fields that might also belong in the target; moving one method can reveal further cohesion improvements. A common pitfall is moving only one method and leaving supporting fields behind; be prepared to follow the trail and move fields or extract a class if many dependencies are involved. Finally, check for circular dependencies after moving code — if the moved method needs types from its old home, consider applying other refactorings or interfaces to break the cycle. The pragmatic goal is to make behavior live where it naturally belongs and ensure tests confirm no behavioral regressions.

keyIdea.title: Move Method Steps
keyIdea.text: Tests → copy method → adapt to local state → run tests → update callers → remove forwarding or deprecate.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.5 › Move Method Steps
Move Method — Process Flow
1. Tests
Cover the method so behavior is verified during change.
2. Copy
Duplicate the method into the target class and adapt references to local fields.
3. Run tests
Run the suite, fix issues, iterate until green.
4. Clean up
Update callers and remove or forward the original method for compatibility.
Concrete example

Copy a calculate_final_price(product) method into Product as calculate_final_price(self), change product.get_price() to self.price and run tests to confirm results match.

Check your understanding

If moving the method introduces tight coupling back to the original class, consider Extract Class or interfaces instead of a direct move.

Key Takeaway

Follow the copy-and-test pattern to move behavior safely and keep public APIs stable when needed.

screens.title: Move Field — moving data to the owner
screens.narratorSegment: Move Field is the companion to Move Method: if a field is primarily consumed by another class, it should live with its primary user. The sequence resembles Move Method but adds constructor and access changes. First, verify the field's usage: if most operations on the value occur in a different class, move the field. Next, add the field to the target class and update its constructor or initialization so the field is created with correct state. Update all local reads and writes to reference the new location, and provide accessors only if necessary. Run tests to catch missing updates. Watch carefully for circular dependencies: moving a field can create a need for types from the original class. If that occurs, refactor with interfaces or introduce an intermediate data object. A common mistake is moving the field but leaving many scattered getters in the old class — prefer to remove redundant accessors and centralize behavior where it belongs. Always run the test suite and consider leaving a forwarding accessor for a short deprecation period if the field is part of a public A P I.

keyIdea.title: Move Field Summary
keyIdea.text: Move fields to the class that primarily uses them, update construction and access, and watch for circular dependencies.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.5 › Move Field
When to move a field

If most reads and writes for a field occur from another class, the field likely belongs with that class.

Steps
  1. Add the field to the target class and initialize it.
  2. Update constructor and call sites to pass or create the value there.
  3. Run tests and remove old accessors or leave forwarding for compatibility.
Concrete example
If shipping_cost_per_item is only used by OrderProcessor, move it from Order to a ShippingDetails object that Order contains, or directly into OrderProcessor if that makes semantic sense and avoids circularity.
Warning
Moving a field without updating related methods often breaks behavior. Tests will catch this — use them early and often.
Design note

If moving the field creates a back-and-forth dependency, consider extracting a small value object so both classes can reference the same data without circular references.

Key Takeaway

Move fields when they are primarily used by another class, but guard against circular dependencies by using small value objects or interfaces.

screens.title: Product & DiscountCalculator — original
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concise Python example that shows Feature Envy. We have a Product class that stores price and discount percentage, and a DiscountCalculator class with a calculate_final_price method that takes a Product and calls product. get_price() and product. get_discount_percentage(). The calculator holds no relevant state. This is classic Feature Envy: the method is more interested in Product's internals than in its own class. The practical consequence is that any change to Product's pricing logic will require touching DiscountCalculator. A better design is to move the calculation into Product so the product is responsible for its own pricing. Notice one misconception people have: they think creating helper classes centralizes logic. Here, the helper simply proxies access. Moving the method into Product removes the need for getters and keeps pricing rules with the data. In a large codebase, these small misplacements multiply and make refactors costly. We'll show the exact code in the visual, then refactor it in the next screen so you can compare before and after and run your tests to ensure behavior remains identical. Product & DiscountCalculator — original means discountcalculator reads product internals through accessors — the calculation belongs on product.. In practical terms, a python example that demonstrates feature envy.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Before: Envy Example
keyIdea.text: DiscountCalculator reads Product internals through accessors — the calculation belongs on Product.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.5 › Product Example — Before
Original code
class Product:
    def __init__(self, name, price, discount_percentage):
        self.name = name
        self.price = price
        self.discount_percentage = discount_percentage

    def get_price(self):
        return self.price

    def get_discount_percentage(self):
        return self.discount_percentage

class DiscountCalculator:
    def calculate_final_price(self, product: Product):
        base_price = product.get_price()
        discount = base_price * product.get_discount_percentage()
        final_price = base_price - discount
        print(f"Calculating final price for {product.name}: {base_price} - {discount} = {final_price}")
        return final_price
Explanation
  • This calculator method depends entirely on Product's internals.
  • DiscountCalculator holds no pricing state — it merely reads Product.
  • Moving the method to Product reduces the number of getters and improves cohesion.
Concrete scenario

When discount rules change, you must update both Product and DiscountCalculator if the logic remains in the calculator.

Key Takeaway

This design places pricing logic separate from the data it needs — a classic smell to fix by moving the method.

screens.title: Product — after Move Method
screens.narratorSegment: Here is the refactored version: the calculate_final_price method now lives on Product and uses self. price and self. discount_percentage directly. This change eliminates the need for get_price and get_discount_percentage for this behavior, and keeps pricing logic next to the data. After moving, callers call laptop. calculate_final_price() rather than passing the product into a separate calculator. This reduces the public surface area and makes it easier to change pricing rules. A subtle but important point: if the old method was part of a public A P I used by other modules, you might keep a forwarding method in the original class for a deprecation period. That minimizes abrupt A P I breaks. Always run tests after each change: moving the method should not alter results. The refactor also makes it easier to extend pricing logic because internal helpers can now be private and use internal fields directly. The result is clearer responsibility: Product owns pricing decisions. The closing question to ask yourself is: if a bug in pricing appears, where should you look first? After this refactor, the answer should be Product.

Refactored code

Order contains items, tax rate, and shipping cost per item, and OrderProcessor. calculate_final_order_total reads several pieces of Order's data: total item price, number of items, tax rate, and shipping cost. This method performs shipping and tax calculations while Order acts mostly as a data holder. This pattern causes Feature Envy because the processor has to know the order's pricing details. The immediate sign is multiple calls to order. get_total_item_price(), order. get_number_of_items(), and so on. The refactor approach is to move the calculation into Order so it becomes responsible for producing its final total. That reduces external knowledge of Order's internals and centralizes pricing rules. A misconception to avoid is assuming processors always belong outside; processors are useful when coordinating multiple entities, but when logic is about a single entity's data, the entity should own that logic. We'll refactor this next and show how to simplify getters and test the behavior before and after moving the method. That reduces external knowledge of Order's internals and centralizes pricing rules. A misconception to avoid is assuming processors always belong outside; processors are useful when coordinating multiple entities, but when logic is about a single entity's data, the entity should own that logic. We'll refactor this next and show how to simplify getters and test the behavior before and after moving the method. Module 07 › Chapter 7.5 › Order Example — Before
Code excerpt
class Order:
    def __init__(self, order_id, items, customer_address, shipping_cost_per_item=5.0):
        self.order_id = order_id
        self.items = items
        self.customer_address = customer_address
        self.shipping_cost_per_item = shipping_cost_per_item
        self.tax_rate = 0.08

    def get_total_item_price(self):
        return sum(item['price'] * item['quantity'] for item in self.items)

class OrderProcessor:
    def calculate_final_order_total(self, order: Order):
        total_items_price = order.get_total_item_price()
        num_items = order.get_number_of_items()
        tax_rate = order.get_tax_rate()
        shipping_cost_per_item = order.get_shipping_cost_per_item()
        ...
Why this is Feature Envy
  • Multiple accessor calls indicate the processor is operating on Order's data model.
  • OrderProcessor's role is primarily a coordinator, but here it owns single-entity calculations.
  • Refactoring moves responsibility into Order improves cohesion and readability.
Concrete scenario

When shipping rules or tax calculation change, centralizing in Order prevents scattered updates.

screens.title: Refactor Order: Move Method
screens.narratorSegment: To refactor the Order example, follow the safe sequence. First, write tests that assert the final total for representative orders, including multiple items and shipping. With tests in place, copy calculate_final_order_total into Order as calculate_final_total(self). Replace calls like order. get_total_item_price() with self. get_total_item_price() or internal computation using self. items, and replace shipping and tax accessors with direct field use if appropriate. Run tests and iterate until they pass. Once green, update any callers to call order. calculate_final_total() and remove or replace the original method in OrderProcessor. If OrderProcessor still coordinates multi-entity workflows, it can call order. calculate_final_total() as a single step. Pay attention to helper getters: if they were only used by the moved method, consider making them private or inlining them inside Order. A common pitfall is forgetting to remove duplicated code in OrderProcessor; leaving redundant logic can hide divergence over time. After refactoring, the pricing logic is co-located with the data it uses, so future changes to shipping, tax, or item pricing are easier to implement and test. Ask yourself: after this change, where should a bug in the total calculation be fixed? The clear answer should be Order.

Module 07 › Chapter 7.5 › Refactor Order
Refactoring steps
  1. Add calculate_final_total(self) to Order.
  2. Adapt logic to use self.items, self.shipping_cost_per_item, and self.tax_rate directly.
  3. Run tests and update callers to use order.calculate_final_total().
  4. Remove or forward the original method in OrderProcessor.
Example refactor (conceptual)
class Order:
    def calculate_final_total(self):
        total_items_price = sum(item['price'] * item['quantity'] for item in self.items)
        shipping_total = sum(item['quantity'] for item in self.items) * self.shipping_cost_per_item
        subtotal = total_items_price + shipping_total
        tax = subtotal * self.tax_rate
        return subtotal + tax
After this change, processors can call order.calculate_final_total() and no longer need to inspect Order internals.

screens.title: Tests and API Stability
screens.narratorSegment: Tests are your primary defense when moving methods or fields. Start by writing unit tests that capture the method's observable behavior and edge cases. When you copy the method into the new class, run tests frequently to discover missing dependencies or subtle differences. If the original method is part of a public A P I, preserve compatibility with a forwarding method that delegates to the new implementation, and mark the old method deprecated only after downstream users migrate. Another safety consideration is circular dependencies: moving a method may require the target class to reference types from the original class, creating a cycle. In that case, introduce a small value object or an interface to break the cycle. Testing strategy should include both unit tests for the moved logic and integration tests that exercise the calling paths. A common mistake is relying solely on manual runs; automated tests run faster and catch regressions earlier. Finally, run the full suite and consider a short compatibility window where both the old and new APIs coexist, documented and tested, before removing the old entry point. This approach minimizes surprises in larger systems.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: There are several recurring mistakes when applying Move Method and Move Field. One is not moving enough related code. Moving a single method without its supporting helpers or fields can leave code split across classes and harder to maintain. Be prepared to follow the trail and relocate related methods or fields. Another is breaking a public A P I unintentionally. If the moved method was relied on externally, provide a thin forwarding method in the original class while clients migrate. A third issue is creating circular dependencies: moving a method to a class that then imports types from its old home can make the dependency graph harder to reason about. To avoid this, extract a small value object or an interface to break the cycle. Misidentifying the right home is also common: if a method uses multiple classes equally, moving it into one can create a new smell. In that situation consider Extract Class instead. Finally, over-reliance on getters and setters can hide poor design; moving behavior back into the owner often allows you to remove unnecessary accessors. Always rely on tests to confirm behavior remains identical after refactoring.

Not moving enough

After moving one method, follow dependencies and move supporting fields or helpers if they belong together.

Breaking APIs

Use forwarding methods to preserve compatibility while clients migrate to the new location.

Circular dependencies

If moving causes cyclic imports, extract a small value object or interface to break the cycle cleanly.

screens.title: When to Move vs Extract Class
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between Move Method, Move Field, and Extract Class is a design decision. Use this checklist: if a method primarily uses one object's data, move it to that object. If a field is primarily consumed by another class, move the field. If the logic depends on several classes roughly equally, prefer Extract Class: create a new collaborator that gathers the necessary data and encapsulates the behavior. Also consider A P I impact: moving a method into a domain object is natural when the operation is conceptually part of that object. If the method coordinates multiple domain objects, it likely belongs in a service or processor, not inside a single domain object. Another factor is coupling: if moving a method introduces dependencies that create cycles, look for an Extract Class or a value object that both classes reference. Finally, use tests and small iterative changes rather than a big rewrite. A clear guiding question is: who owns the data and who can implement the operation without knowing another class's internals? Answering that determines the right refactor. When to Move vs Extract Class means move when one owner dominates. extract when multiple owners share responsibility. use tests and avoid cycles.. screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essentials. First, Feature Envy is a smell where a method spends more time interacting with another object's data than its own. Spot it by noticing many accessor calls to a foreign object. Second, Move Method is the primary refactoring to fix it: copy the method to the target class, adapt it to use local state, run tests, update callers, and remove or forward the original. This keeps behavior close to data. Third, Move Field relocates data to the class that uses it most, but be mindful of constructor and dependency changes and avoid circular dependencies by introducing value objects or interfaces when required. Across all refactors, tests are your safety net and forwarding methods help preserve A P I compatibility during migration. Use these techniques to keep classes cohesive and to minimize coupling so your codebase stays maintainable as requirements evolve.

screens.title: Three Practical Reminders

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we study the Feature Envy code smell and two targeted refactorings: Move Method and Move Field. Feature Envy appears when a method in one class spends more time accessing another class's data than using its own. That pattern leads to tight coupling and weak encapsulation — the behavior lives in the wrong place. You will learn how to detect this smell in real code, how to decide the method's rightful home, and how the Move Method and Move Field refactorings restore cohesion by placing behavior next to the data it needs. We'll use short Python examples to practice. First, I'll show a calculator class reaching into a product for price and discount and how moving that logic into Product clarifies responsibility. Then we'll work through an Order and OrderProcessor example to practice the steps, safety checks, and testing strategies you need before and after a refactor. By the end you'll be able to identify Feature Envy, apply the right move refactoring, and reason about A P I stability and circular dependency risks. Think about a method you recently debugged: does it touch another object's internals repeatedly? That pattern often points to Feature Envy.

These objectives show the skills you'll gain. First, you'll learn to spot Feature Envy: a method that interacts more with another class's data than with its own. We'll practice concrete identification techniques, such as counting accessor calls and noticing empty host classes. Second, you'll explain why Feature Envy makes code brittle — increased coupling and weaker encapsulation — and be able to describe the practical cost when implementations change. Third and fourth, you'll apply two refactorings: Move Method and Move Field. For Move Method, you'll learn a safe sequence: copy the method, adapt to the new class, run tests, and remove the old forwarding method if appropriate. For Move Field, you'll learn to migrate data and update callers while avoiding circular dependencies. Each objective pairs explanation with a small mnemonic so you can recall the pattern during code review. Achieving these objectives helps you improve cohesion, simplify APIs, and reduce the need for getters and setters. After practicing, you'll be able to choose between moving behavior, extracting a new class, or adding a forwarding method when compatibility matters.

Beyond knowing the theory, you will follow a safe, repeatable sequence for moving methods and fields. Start by writing or verifying tests that cover the method's behavior. Next, duplicate the method into the target class and adapt references to use local fields rather than getters. Run tests: if green, remove the original method or replace it with a simple forwarder to preserve A P I compatibility. For moving a field, update constructors and access points, and be mindful of creating circular references. We'll practice with two concrete Python examples: a Product and DiscountCalculator pair, and an Order plus OrderProcessor. These examples let you see both simple and slightly more complex cases where multiple supporting methods and fields need migration. We'll also cover when Extract Class is a better choice if a method uses data from several classes equally. Practicing this sequence repeatedly makes refactoring low-risk and routine, so the codebase becomes easier to evolve over time.

Feature Envy is a code smell where a method in one class is more interested in another class's internals than its own. Practically, you see a method that calls many accessors on a foreign object, rarely using its own fields. This signals the method likely belongs to the other class. For example, a method that repeatedly calls product. get_price(), product. get_discount(), and product. get_name() while holding no relevant state itself demonstrates envy. The behavior indicates a misplaced responsibility. A simple detection strategy is to count how often the method touches another object's data versus its own; if the foreign touches dominate, you have Feature Envy. A common misconception is that adding a helper or utility class is always the solution. Often the correct answer is to move the method to the class whose data it uses — that preserves encapsulation and reduces accessors. Another contrast: if a method uses multiple classes equally, moving it into one will create new coupling; in that case consider Extract Class instead. In short, Feature Envy shows that behavior and data are separated incorrectly — your refactor moves behavior back next to its natural data owner. Think of it as returning work to the owner who has the tools and access to do it correctly.

Feature Envy undermines two core design goals: low coupling and strong encapsulation. When methods live in the wrong class, other classes must know about internal fields and accessors, which ties their implementation details together. If Class A repeatedly inspects Class B's internals, a change to B's data representation may require coordinated edits in A, increasing maintenance cost and the risk of bugs. Encapsulation is weakened because the external class is effectively manipulating the internal state rather than asking the owning class to perform the operation. This reduces clarity about who controls the data and where business rules belong. A helpful contrast is to consider the refactored alternative: move the behavior inside the data owner. Then changes to data layout are localized and the public interface presents a meaningful operation rather than raw access. A common misconception is that writing lots of getters is harmless; in reality getters encourage external classes to implement logic on foreign data instead of delegating the work to the object that owns it. The takeaway is clear: reduce Feature Envy to keep the system modular and resilient to internal change.

Move Method is a focused refactoring: relocate a method from one class to the class whose data it uses. Follow a safe sequence. Step one: ensure you have tests that cover the method's behavior. Tests act as a safety net. Step two: copy the method into the target class and modify it to use local fields and methods instead of foreign accessors. Step three: run tests. If tests pass, adjust call sites to invoke the new location. Step four: remove the original method or leave a thin forwarding method for backward compatibility while deprecating the old signature. Watch for related methods and fields that might also belong in the target; moving one method can reveal further cohesion improvements. A common pitfall is moving only one method and leaving supporting fields behind; be prepared to follow the trail and move fields or extract a class if many dependencies are involved. Finally, check for circular dependencies after moving code — if the moved method needs types from its old home, consider applying other refactorings or interfaces to break the cycle. The pragmatic goal is to make behavior live where it naturally belongs and ensure tests confirm no behavioral regressions.

Move Field is the companion to Move Method: if a field is primarily consumed by another class, it should live with its primary user. The sequence resembles Move Method but adds constructor and access changes. First, verify the field's usage: if most operations on the value occur in a different class, move the field. Next, add the field to the target class and update its constructor or initialization so the field is created with correct state. Update all local reads and writes to reference the new location, and provide accessors only if necessary. Run tests to catch missing updates. Watch carefully for circular dependencies: moving a field can create a need for types from the original class. If that occurs, refactor with interfaces or introduce an intermediate data object. A common mistake is moving the field but leaving many scattered getters in the old class — prefer to remove redundant accessors and centralize behavior where it belongs. Always run the test suite and consider leaving a forwarding accessor for a short deprecation period if the field is part of a public A P I.

Testing strategy should include both unit tests for the moved logic and integration tests that exercise the calling paths. A common mistake is relying solely on manual runs; automated tests run faster and catch regressions earlier. Finally, run the full suite and consider a short compatibility window where both the old and new APIs coexist, documented and tested, before removing the old entry point. This approach minimizes surprises in larger systems.

There are several recurring mistakes when applying Move Method and Move Field. One is not moving enough related code. Moving a single method without its supporting helpers or fields can leave code split across classes and harder to maintain. Be prepared to follow the trail and relocate related methods or fields. Another is breaking a public A P I unintentionally. If the moved method was relied on externally, provide a thin forwarding method in the original class while clients migrate. A third issue is creating circular dependencies: moving a method to a class that then imports types from its old home can make the dependency graph harder to reason about. To avoid this, extract a small value object or an interface to break the cycle. Misidentifying the right home is also common: if a method uses multiple classes equally, moving it into one can create a new smell. In that situation consider Extract Class instead. Finally, over-reliance on getters and setters can hide poor design; moving behavior back into the owner often allows you to remove unnecessary accessors. Always rely on tests to confirm behavior remains identical after refactoring.

Choosing between Move Method, Move Field, and Extract Class is a design decision. Use this checklist: if a method primarily uses one object's data, move it to that object. If a field is primarily consumed by another class, move the field. If the logic depends on several classes roughly equally, prefer Extract Class: create a new collaborator that gathers the necessary data and encapsulates the behavior. Also consider A P I impact: moving a method into a domain object is natural when the operation is conceptually part of that object. If the method coordinates multiple domain objects, it likely belongs in a service or processor, not inside a single domain object. Another factor is coupling: if moving a method introduces dependencies that create cycles, look for an Extract Class or a value object that both classes reference. Let's summarize the essentials. First, Feature Envy is a smell where a method spends more time interacting with another object's data than its own. Spot it by noticing many accessor calls to a foreign object. Second, Move Method is the primary refactoring to fix it: copy the method to the target class, adapt it to use local state, run tests, update callers, and remove or forward the original. This keeps behavior close to data. Third, Move Field relocates data to the class that uses it most, but be mindful of constructor and dependency changes and avoid circular dependencies by introducing value objects or interfaces when required. Across all refactors, tests are your safety net and forwarding methods help preserve A P I compatibility during migration. Use these techniques to keep classes cohesive and to minimize coupling so your codebase stays maintainable as requirements evolve.

Before wrapping up, keep three practical reminders in your toolkit. First, look for many accessor calls to the same object as a red flag of Feature Envy. Second, when you move methods or fields, proceed incrementally with tests and consider leaving thin forwarding methods to avoid breaking clients. Third, if behavior touches multiple classes equally, prefer Extract Class or a small value object rather than forcing a single class to own everything. These practices will help you maintain higher cohesion and lower coupling, making your code easier to change and reason about. When you return to your codebase, run a few small experiments: pick a suspicious method, write a test, move it, and observe how the codebase feels afterward. That hands-on practice is the fastest path to internalizing these refactorings.
